claims.text: The balance between configurational entropy and local chemical interactions governs structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
Favorable Al-Ni pair correlations can drive local chemical short-range order or clustering in Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloys.
The extent of local chemical short-range order determines whether an alloy remains homogeneous and single-phase or develops clustering or phase separation under thermal stress.
The proposed starting nanoparticles are near-equimolar, single-phase Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni solid solutions.
Rapid synthesis can produce the proposed nanoparticles with initially minimal short-range order.
Rapid quenching minimizes additional short-range-order development.
Slow annealing enhances the formation of local short-range order.
Increasing temperature reduces the strength of chemical clustering or pair correlations.
At high temperature, thermal energy increases atomic mobility and can overcome favorable local pair interactions.
Overcoming local pair interactions at high temperature maintains a near-random solid solution stabilized by high configurational entropy.
When short-range order develops, favorable local interactions promote clustering, early-stage phase segregation, and destabilization of the entropy-stabilized state.
The preexisting level of short-range order mediates the nanoalloy's response to subsequent high-temperature exposure.
Rapidly quenched, low-SRO nanoalloys will remain more homogeneous and single-phase than slowly annealed, high-SRO nanoalloys after identical high-temperature treatment.
Slowly annealed nanoalloys will show more detectable clustering or incipient phase separation after high-temperature treatment.
The prediction is restricted to equimolar nanoalloys that initially form single-phase solid solutions and are exposed below their melting points for times permitting measurable diffusion.
Alloy-specific interaction strengths and processing history bound the proposed effect of short-range order on stability.
Critical temperatures and timescales for short-range-order evolution may vary with alloy system and particle size.

A lack of statistically significant differences in SRO, clustering, and phase stability between the two processing groups would falsify the claim that initial SRO governs high-temperature stability under the tested conditions.
